..
KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

An upper-level trough axis is currently located over the region
which has led to isolated/scattered over much of the higher
terrain across New Hampshire and western Maine. This activity
should increase in coverage through the afternoon. A few
thunderstorms will also be possible with some weak instability
in place. SPC mesoanalysis suggests MLCAPE will only max out in
the 250 to 500 J/kg range with very weak shear. Thus, any
isolated storms that do form should be fairly tame. That being
said, brief gusty winds will be possible under any showers or
storms that move overhead. 

Any showers or storms will diminish quickly with the loss of
daytime heating, giving way to more valley fog overnight and
maybe some marine fog. Lows will mainly be in the 50s. 

High pressure moves in overnight into Wednesday as an upper-
level ridge axis moves into the region. This will lead to dry 
conditions and warmer temperatures. Highs will mainly range from
the low/mid 70s north, to the low/mid 80s across the south and 
along the coast.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...
Clouds build and dewpoints rise during the day Thursday as a 
trough approaches the region. Most of the area should remain dry
as the 25.12Z NAM Nest and RRFS suggest just a chance for some 
isolated to scattered showers as the warm front approaches. The 
best chance is over New Hampshire as Maine looks to remain on 
the periphery of high pressure departing to the east. High 
temperatures climb into the low 80s just about everywhere, with 
dewpoints in the mid-60s making it feel somewhat sticky.

The first of two cold fronts attempts to make a pass Thursday 
night which will increase PoPs for the western half of the CWA, 
but most of the eastern half of and coast hold on to 30-40% PoPs
as the NAM and RRFS suggests this front washes out before 
making it too far. Depending on how this shakes out Friday 
morning could feature plenty of fog and drizzle as it wont to 
much to budge dew points. This along with lingering cloud cover 
may act to stunt development of anything during the day Friday. 
Interestingly, the RRFS which tends to be an aggressive model 
is not currently suggesting much more than scattered showers and
storms. Long range probabilities of rainfall greater than a 
half inch continue to fall with much of the area given a 25 to 
35 percent chance by the NBM and only about a 10 to 15 percent 
chance among the ECMWF and GFS blends. Higher probabilities 
exist in the mountains where orographic lift will help rainfall 
rates. Otherwise, it looks like that, outside of a good 
thunderstorm, many locations are only going to see around a 
tenth to a quarter of an inch. Certainly not the trend we wanted
to see drought-wise, but I can't say I am surprised as this has
been a persistent trend all Summer. CSU's machine learning 
model maintains low probabilities for severe storms Friday, but 
as mentioned if little instability is able to develop, that 
won't be much of a concern.

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...
The front is progged to clear the area by Saturday morning and 
it's progression is going to have an impact on Friday nights low
temperatures. If the front clears the mountains overnight, we 
could see temperatures radiate down into the upper 40s. The 
foothills may see temperatures fall into the low to mid- 50s, 
and the coastal plain is less likely to clear out much and more 
likely to see temperatures only fall into the upper 50s and even
low 60s on the immediate coast. Drier air does quickly fill in 
Saturday with high pressure building in at the surface. This 
makes for a mostly sunny and precipitation free weekend with 
high temperatures in the mid-70s to low 80s and dewpoints in the
50s across much of the area.

Global models suggest at least one upper low moves through 
Quebec Sunday making its closest pass Sunday night which may 
drag a front through the region early next week. There is still 
plenty of uncertainty among the global models on exactly how 
this plays out, but I think the chance PoPs from the NBM are 
fair.
